The authors propose a new 'analogue transformation' method for controlling waves in different branches of physics, including acoustics.
The key insight is that the acoustic wave equation is structurally identical to the equation describing a relativistic massless scalar field over a curved spacetime.

The standard transformation acoustics (STA) approach has several drawbacks, including non-invariance under transformations mixing space and time, inability to deal with non-zero background fluid velocity, and difficulty in achieving simultaneous increases in sound speed and density.
The new method allows for transformations that mix space and time, which was not possible with the standard STA approach.
The authors demonstrate the power of their method by designing a dynamic compressor, an acoustic spacetime cloak, and a carpet cloak for a moving aircraft.
The acoustic spacetime cloak can conceal certain spacetime events by speeding up or slowing down the propagation of sound waves.
The new method allows the required transformation of the background fluid velocity, enabling the design of a carpet cloak that can effectively conceal a bump on a moving aircraft.

The analogue approach obtains the opposite behavior compared to STA, where an increase in density corresponds to a decrease in sound speed and vice versa, which is more in line with current acoustic metamaterials.
The authors note that the method can be applied to any system that provides an analogue model of a relativistic field, such as phonons in Bose-Einstein condensates and graphene.
The equations used by the authors do not contain any approximations apart from those necessary to obtain the original wave equation, allowing the method to work in both the wave and eikonal regimes.
The designed carpet cloak does not introduce reflections, as the employed transformation is continuous at the boundaries.

The key steps in the analogue transformation method are: 1) Identify a virtual medium, 2) Map the laboratory equation to an analogue equation, 3) Transform the analogue equation, 4) Rename the coordinates, and 5) Map the renamed equation back to laboratory space.

The local manipulability of the propagating (meta)media will be crucial for the practical implementation of the method, which can be achieved through techniques like controlling the conductivity in graphene.
The authors state that their results indicate the idea underlying transformation optics has an even farther-reaching scope than initially foreseen.
The method is general and could be considered as a new paradigm for controlling waves in different branches of physics, from acoustics in quantum fluids to graphene electronics.
